title: China is weathering the Hormuz energy crisis. But copying its model comes with risks
gist: China absorbed the Strait of Hormuz oil shock better than any other major importer by combining ~1.4 billion barrels of stockpiles with an electrified economy (EVs were >60% of H1 2026 domestic vehicle sales), validating its decade-long 'green energy statecraft'. The article argues Europe must copy the electrification hedge but be selective about which parts of the clean-tech stack it buys from Beijing, given China's 90%+ control of solar and rare earth supply chains.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz crisis forced the 32 IEA member states into their largest-ever emergency stock release, totalling more than 400 million barrels including 172 million from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, to replace part of the 20 million b/d that had been transiting Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: SPR and IEA reserves are now materially drawn down, so the developed world's buffer against a second shock is thinner — watch refill buying as a structural bid under crude.
insights.quote: They released more than 400 million barrels in total, including 172 million from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, to replace some of the 20 million barrels per day (b/d) that had been passing through Hormuz.
insights.locator: Weathering the storm

insights.claim: China entered the Hormuz crisis with roughly 1.4 billion barrels of oil in storage — about 360 million in government reserves and the remainder commercial — equal to at least three months of imports, and therefore required no participation in the IEA's collective release.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: China's commercial tank overhang means Beijing can sit out price spikes and re-enter as a buyer only when it chooses, dampening the upside of supply-shock oil trades.
insights.quote: Beijing entered the crisis with an estimated 1.4 billion barrels in storage: around 360 million in government reserves and the rest in commercial tanks, totalling at least three months of imports.
insights.locator: China needed no such collective effort

insights.claim: China's crude imports fell by a third during the crisis, from 12 million b/d on the eve of the war to under 8 million b/d in May and June 2026, with only about one-third of lost Gulf barrels replaced from alternative suppliers such as Brazil.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A 4 million b/d demand hole in the world's largest importer is a bearish offset to a bullish supply shock — model crude balances with Chinese demand destruction, not just barrels lost at the chokepoint.
insights.quote: China’s crude imports fell by a third, from 12 million b/d on the eve of the war to less than 8 million b/d in May and June.
insights.locator: The rest of these lost imports went unreplaced

insights.claim: About 60 per cent of China's unreplaced import shortfall was covered by drawing storage while the remainder became a genuine fall in oil burned, achieved by cutting refinery crude runs and ordering state refiners to halt fuel exports so domestic supply was prioritized.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A Chinese export halt removes a major source of diesel and gasoline from Asian markets — refining margins and product cracks outside China are the second-order trade in any Hormuz-style event.
insights.quote: Refineries cut their crude runs and Beijing ordered the big state refiners to halt fuel exports so that what they did produce stayed at home.
insights.locator: About 60 per cent of the shortfall

insights.claim: The oil importer most structurally exposed to a Hormuz closure — China imports 70 per cent of its oil, around half of that from the Gulf — turned out to be the least disrupted by the crisis, inverting the usual exposure-equals-vulnerability assumption.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Import-dependence ratios are a poor proxy for energy vulnerability; reprice country risk on stockpile depth plus electrification rate instead.
insights.quote: The oil importer most exposed to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz – China imports 70 per cent of its oil, around half of it from the Gulf – has also been the least disrupted.
insights.locator: But the numbers support their conclusions

insights.claim: Electrification lets an economy cut oil consumption without cutting transport activity, which is the mechanism that allowed China to absorb a one-third drop in crude imports without an economic stop.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat EV penetration as a macro shock-absorber metric: high-penetration economies have lower oil-price pass-through to GDP and inflation.
insights.quote: An electrified economy can use less oil without using less transport.
insights.locator: Electrification and security

insights.claim: Electric vehicles accounted for more than 60 per cent of China's domestic monthly vehicle sales in the first half of 2026, with drivers of conventional cars reportedly switching to electric ride-hailing during the fuel squeeze.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese gasoline demand has a structural ceiling — long-dated Asian gasoline demand forecasts and refinery capex premised on Chinese growth are exposed.
insights.quote: Electric vehicles accounted for more than 60 per cent of domestic monthly vehicle sales in the first half of 2026.
insights.locator: Electrification and security

insights.claim: In the first half of 2026 alone China added more wind capacity than in any full calendar year before 2025, extending its lead in global renewable power installation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese turbine and grid-equipment volumes keep compressing global equipment costs — a headwind for Western OEM pricing power and a tailwind for project IRRs that buy Chinese.
insights.quote: In the first half of 2026, China added more wind capacity than in any full calendar year before 2025.
insights.locator: Chinese clean technology has been manufactured

insights.claim: China's energy resilience was a deliberate strategic design rather than a climate-policy side effect, traceable to Hu Jintao's 2003 'Malacca Dilemma' framing of chokepoint risk that has underpinned Beijing's low-carbon industrial strategy ever since.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese clean-tech policy support should be modelled as national-security spending, which is far less likely to be cut than subsidy programmes framed as climate policy.
insights.quote: This resilience is not a happy coincidence or an unintended benefit of climate policy.
insights.locator: This resilience is not a happy coincidence

insights.claim: China's 15th Five Year Plan (2026-2030), adopted in March, formalizes green energy statecraft by targeting stable annual crude output of 200 million tonnes, increased oil and gas reserves, petroleum consumption replacement, and secured supply of critical minerals for new energy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The plan is a five-year procurement roadmap: expect sustained state bid for critical-mineral assets and domestic upstream capex alongside, not instead of, electrification.
insights.quote: increasing oil and gas reserves and production, stabilizing annual crude oil output at 200 million tonnes, replacing petroleum consumption, and securing the supply of critical mineral resources for new energy
insights.locator: China's 15th Five Year Plan

insights.claim: Writing in the CCP's flagship theoretical journal Qiushi on 1 September 2026, Zhao Hongtu and Chen Wenlin argued resources are no longer 'king' in energy and that countries controlling transition-related technology, finance and rules will out-leverage mineral-rich economies as the 'electrostate' rises.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Beijing is publicly reframing energy power as control of technology and standards rather than reserves — expect Chinese policy to defend manufacturing and rule-setting positions over resource acquisition where the two conflict.
insights.quote: Mineral-rich economies may have some leverage, but the countries that control ‘transition-related technology, finance and rules’ will gain more influence
insights.locator: Resources are no longer 'king'

insights.claim: Chinese state theorists claim the US-Israeli war on Iran has elevated energy security to a top national policymaking priority and made clean energy a recognized security route, with transition-embracing economies expected to gain position in the future global energy order.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Post-Iran-war, clean-energy buildout in importing nations is driven by security budgets rather than climate politics, which broadens and stabilizes the demand base.
insights.quote: economies that actively embrace the energy transition may occupy more important positions in the future global energy landscape
insights.locator: As a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran

insights.claim: Electrification functions as a hedge against three distinct risks simultaneously — volatile commodity pricing, a weaponized dollar, and general geopolitical uncertainty — which is why it appeals to governments beyond any climate rationale.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Dollar-invoiced oil dependence is itself a sanctions vector, so de-dollarization and electrification are the same trade for many emerging markets.
insights.quote: electrification helps governments to hedge against volatile pricing, a weaponized dollar, and an increasingly uncertain geopolitical environment
insights.locator: The plan's approach is convincing

insights.claim: In 2024 China produced more than 90 per cent of the world's polysilicon, wafers and cells and 86 per cent of solar modules, with comparable concentration in batteries including graphite and anode active materials.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Any solar or battery supply-chain diversification thesis starts from near-total Chinese share, so non-Chinese capacity additions are priced against a structurally lower-cost incumbent.
insights.quote: In 2024, China produced more than 90 per cent of the polysilicon, wafers and cells, and 86 per cent of the modules needed for solar energy globally.
insights.locator: China's dominance of renewables

insights.claim: Southeast Asian nations spent over $20 billion on Chinese-made clean-tech products in 2026 to date, while Indonesia's president has pushed an all-electric transport transition specifically to cut import reliance.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: ASEAN is the marginal growth market for Chinese clean-tech exports — a channel that partly offsets Western tariff barriers for Chinese manufacturers.
insights.locator: This is particularly clear for Asian economies

insights.claim: China financed approximately $20.1 billion of green energy across the Global South in the first half of 2026, exceeding its total for all of 2025.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese project finance locks in Chinese equipment standards in emerging markets, entrenching supply-chain lock-in ahead of any Western alternative.
insights.quote: China is also financing green energy at record levels across the Global South, totalling approximately $20.1 billion in the first half of 2026, more than all of 2025.
insights.locator: China is also financing green energy

insights.claim: China demonstrated willingness to weaponize clean-tech inputs by halting rare earth exports to Japan in January amid Taiwan-related tensions, and could similarly leverage its dominance in solar panels, EVs and other green technologies.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Rare-earth and component export controls are a live, demonstrated tool — price tail risk into any manufacturer dependent on single-source Chinese inputs.
insights.locator: Different dependencies

insights.claim: Dependence on Chinese low-carbon technology carries a different risk profile from fossil-fuel dependence: it does not produce an immediate price shock but instead constrains a country's ability to execute its energy transition over time.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Clean-tech dependency shows up as delayed capacity and slipped project timelines rather than a spot-price spike — a slow-burn risk that commodity-style hedges cannot cover.
insights.quote: No navy can blockade the sun or wind.
insights.locator: This risk is different to that

insights.claim: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen stated in her State of the Union that Europe is more than 80 per cent dependent on China for many critical raw materials and 90 per cent for some rare earths, and called for urgent procurement and reserve building.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: An explicit EU commitment to build critical-mineral reserves signals state-backed offtake demand — bullish for non-Chinese refining and stockpiling capacity.
insights.quote: We are more than 80 per cent dependent on China for many critical raw materials. 90 per cent for some rare earths… We need to urgently procure and build up our reserves.
insights.locator: Europe needs to think strategically

insights.claim: Europe should selectively secure critical components rather than rebuilding the entire clean-tech supply chain, the approach already shown by tightening rules around inverters.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Policy support will concentrate in chokepoint components like inverters and grid controls rather than spreading across modules and cells — target the narrow segments, not broad domestic manufacturing plays.
insights.quote: It means being selective, as Europe has demonstrated by tightening the rules around critical components like inverters.
insights.locator: Europe should not slow its transition

insights.claim: This autumn EU officials must simultaneously settle the bloc's trade posture towards China and finalize the Industrial Accelerator Act rules aimed at boosting European manufacturing, with the UK facing a parallel set of competition, security and decarbonization questions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A near-dated policy catalyst for European clean-tech manufacturers and Chinese exporters alike — watch the Industrial Accelerator Act's local-content and trade provisions this autumn.
insights.locator: This autumn, EU officials will face

insights.claim: European diversification is also a hedge against US policy volatility, with officials warning the Trump administration could use Europe's dependency on American gas as leverage to dictate terms on issues such as Greenland or tariffs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: European LNG contracting decisions now carry a political-risk discount on US supply, supporting diversification premiums for non-US cargoes and domestic electrification.
insights.locator: Done right, this should not only reduce

insights.claim: Because both the US and China have demonstrated they will weaponize energy supply, a Europe without comparable leverage will have its energy choices dictated externally, implying Europe must develop its own geoeconomic deterrent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect escalating EU use of trade instruments and reserve powers — regulatory risk rises for firms sitting between the three blocs' supply chains.
insights.quote: Both the US and China have shown they will use supply as a weapon; a Europe that cannot answer in kind will have its energy choices made for it.
insights.locator: Perhaps it's time for Europe
